claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game restricts item placement to specific developer-intended spots rather than allowing free-form organization.

citations.review_text: i thought this was going to be a game where i can unpack my belongings into this room it gives me however I personally like, and thats why i thought it was a relaxing game, but once i found out you had to put things in certain spots i honestly lost all interest in it. The game went from relaxing to really annoying trying to find where certain things (some of which, i didnt even know what they were) went in this room(s)

3/10, I did not like this game at all and couldn't bring myself to finish it for multiple reasons.

I walked in thinking that it would be a calming organization sim in which you would be able to choose where you want to put things. Instead, it acts like a puzzle game, in which you are given a ton of items and very limited space to put them, a trait only exacerbated by the fact that there are perfectly reasonable places for items that are just completely invalid for some reason.

I know that there is an option to enable "put things wherever," but for some reason it's under accessibility, which seems like a not-so-subtle nudge by the devs to make you feel incompetent for not following their rules. The original, unaltered version of the game feels less like a game of choice and aesthetic freedom and more like a "guess where the game wants you to put this doll" simulator.

I also feel like the choice to make the items sort of "reveal" the personality of the character that, I guess, you are playing as(?), was a somewhat bad decision. Part of the draw of the concept of a game built around organization is that in organization you can express yourself, a bit like art. In forcing the items to be very specific to the character you are organizing for it takes away some of the creative potential of the game in my opinion.

Overall a good premise with subpar execution and a lot of iffy design choices. I wouldn't buy unless you like somewhat unintuitive puzzles and would relate a lot to the character you are organizing for.

it certainly doesn't deserve a negative review since the overall game is incredly fun, but it's rathet limited in how and where you're allowed to place things.
it's quite sad cause it changes the game from a relaxing game to a tedious puzzle game as you try to find out where the game wants you  to place a third of the items you've placed down.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game tells a story entirely through environment and objects without text or dialogue, following a character through different stages of life.

citations.review_text: Unpacking is a sweet little game. It is very short, and for $20 that is a little insane for only 4 hours of content. However, if you can grab this one on a sale then it is worth it. It is a calm cozy game, with very well done environmental story telling, following the story of growing up with a girl throughout her life. Nice, short, sweet. Get it on sale and you got a good deal.

Very sweet game that makes amazing use of environmental storytelling. My selfish wish is that I had an endless supply of rooms to unpack. That being said I appreciate the exceptionally well executed ones we got
I love the way the story is told only by the objects.. it is brilliant!

Such an incredible work of art.  The fact that it's able to tell such a poignant story about personal growth without a single line of dialogue is impressively beautiful.  Really hope we get sequels to this that take us through other people's lives spanning several decades while retaining the signature cozy gameplay loop.

Another gem! A very short but engaging cozy game. We indirectly follow the life story of the character, from the baby stages to the adulthood, while unpacking after each house move, discovery what's been kept, what's been left behind and what's been added.
Honestly it took me by surprise, I wasn't expecting any story at all for a game like this

Un petit jeu cozy, court, très simple, mais tellement satisfaisant !

Chaque niveau vous demande de déballer des cartons et d'en ranger le contenu dans une ou plusieurs pièces d'une maison.

D'abord, l'expérience utilisateur est juste parfaite. Les contrôles, les signaux visuels, tout est simple mais tellement ergonomique et bien pensé. On prend un vrai plaisir à placer, déplacer et redéplacer les objets pour parvenir à la configuration idéale et qui nous convient.

Mais c'est quoi la configuration idéale ? Eh bien le jeu laisse libre court à votre imagination pour cela. Alors certes il y a un petit aspect puzzle (vous ne pouvez pas mettre une brosse à dents dans la cuisine par exemple), et vous devrez parfois empiler les objets de manière astucieuse pour avoir assez de place (notamment dans les niveaux plus petits, style appartement), mais ce n'est pas difficile et il est impossible de perdre dans Unpacking - prenez votre temps et rangez à votre rythme.

Enfin, le coup de génie de Unpacking, c'est de nous faire suivre au fil des niveaux la vie d'une personne, qui nous est racontée au travers de ses déménagements et emménagements. Pas de texte, pas de dialogue, non. Juste le gameplay décrit précédemment. Et pourtant en rangeant les objets, on découvre réellement qui est cette personne et les étapes importantes traversées au fil des années.

En résumé, le jeu est un peu court, ne propose pas de challenge, mais chaque minute passée dessus est un plaisir - tout ce qu'on demande d'un jeu cozy.

Unpacking is a relaxing and cozy game with a simple but unique concept. It tells its story without dialogue, letting you learn about the character through the items you unpack.  
the game has a calm atmosphere. It’s short, enjoyable, and worth trying if you’re looking for something different.

Unpacking is short, sweet, and really charming! I'm very impressed by the amount of narrative and emotion the creators were able to convey just through the environmental storytelling. I wasn't expecting to have an emotional reaction to this game, but I quickly grew attached to our protagonist and found myself happy for her, angry for her, and proud of her.

The game is also great mechanically, especially if you're the kind of person who likes to sort things and line them up nicely. There are a lot of different objects to unpack, and they all make very satisfying clinks, taps, and thunks when you put them down. There were a few objects I didn't recognize, but I had no trouble finding out what they were by searching online real quick.

The music is relaxing and the art is beautiful and immersive. I had a great time with this game, and I expect to enjoy it just as much on a replay, too.

I have played through this game many times over the years of owning it. It is one of my favorite cozy games and just brings me so much joy to play. I love this type of indirect story telling where you learn about the character simply by seeing what they own. From childhood hobbies and toys, to young adult college dreams, to bad relationships and self discovery, to a much deserved happy ending. So much can be gleamed from little books and figurines pulled out of boxes. 

I would LOVE for the devs to share more stories in sequel games, I would play EVERY SINGLE ONE! I have said it so many times to friends when recommending this game to them that I would love a series of this. I commend you all for creating such an amazing game and to those who are indecisive, buy it!

claims.claim: Reviewers describe restriction in item placement where certain objects must go into specific locations, such as kitchen items in cabinets rather than on countertops, causing frustration for some.

citations.review_text: Sweet game, reminds me of the flash decorating games I used to play as a kid. It's pretty easy to navigate but can be exhausting at times to have to figure out the "right" way to place things (the kitchen frustrated me the most because apparently pots have to be stored in cabinets and are not allowed to be on the countertop). Other than that, the story is quite nice, and there's a bunch of lore which you can unpack on Reddit if you're interested.

I liked being able to get a sense of the course of a person’s life from their belongings. Although there were times when it was hard to understand why a particular item shouldn’t be placed there, it was still fun.

Grade: C-
Do you enjoy organizing other people’s junk?
Do you have competitive OCD?
If the answer is yes to either of these, congratulations! Unpacking is GOTY baby! Ten out of ten! Every award! Move over, It Take’s Two! Review over.

If the answer is no... 
Congratulations! You just saved yourself a few annoying hours because Unpacking is the part of moving house that everyone resents in real life—except without the pizza, friends, or any of your own stuff. It’s a game that bravely asks the questions other developers are too afraid to ask like:
“Where does this mug go?”
“How about this cushion?”
“What about this pig mascot plush I’ve been carrying through five different apartments because apparently emotional attachment is stronger than common sense?”
And the best part? It’s the same items at every location plus a few more! Art imitating life! The accumulation of junk as you get older and refusing to throw any of it away.

Now for the gameplay. (It’s a short section). 
Drag object from Box A to Surface B until the game nods in approval. The placement rules don’t matter… except when they do. Book? Anywhere. Controller? Sure. Mug? Living room? Why not. Coffee pot? Counter only. Do not put it in the cabinet. Walkie-talkies? Closet drawer of course. Clothing basket? Keep guessing.

And what about the story? 
It’s all visual, which is kinda neat, but it landed somewhere between heartfelt indie storytelling and “I’m 14 and this is deep.”
“Oh, she went to college.”
“Oh, she moved in with a guy.”
“Oh, he sucks.”
“Oh, now she’s living alone.”
“Oh, now she’s in an LGBTQ+ relationship, and that probably should’ve been tagged.”
I’m sure it’s all very touching, but halfway through I stopped following her emotional journey and started speedrunning the task.

Final verdict: I don’t know what I was expecting, but this isn’t it. People own way too much stuff, and I apparently don’t enjoy organizing it for them. The only thing missing was someone asking me to help carry a couch up t…

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game tells its story entirely without words or dialogue through items and environmental details.

citations.review_text: this game was so incredibly relaxing! the storytelling is amazing throughout, so much is said without words and somehow it makes the game carry so much more meaning. there's a clear appreciation for the smallest of details within every aspect of game design even down to the amazing music and i really enjoyed that. i definitely recommend this to anyone looking for a cozy game that is more than the normal routine grind. i still play this game when i get stressed and it works so well to calm me down and ground me in something beautiful!

Moving through a story without words could be daunting for anyone, but Unpacking does it effortlessly. You follow our main character through her life, hers ups and downs. Tidying, organizing and, yes, unpacking at every step. It's a game that you'll play over and over again.

From the moment you open your first box, the world slows down. There’s no pressure, no timers, no overwhelming mechanics, just the gentle, almost therapeutic act of taking items out of boxes and finding a place for them. It’s simple in the best way, like tidying a space while your mind quietly unwinds after a long day.

There’s barely any dialogue, no big dramatic cutscenes, yet somehow, it tells one of the most human, emotional stories I’ve experienced in a game. You follow someone’s life not through words, but through their belongings. A childhood bedroom turns into a dorm, then into shared spaces, heartbreak, independence, and eventually something soft and whole again. The gameplay itself is incredibly satisfying. Placing items “just right” scratches that cozy, organised itch, and the soft soundtrack wraps everything in a calm, comforting atmosphere. It’s the kind of game you can play while half curled up, half zoning out, and still feel completely immersed. Many players describe it as “relaxing and therapeutic,” with a calming loop of organising and decorating .

What I love most is how safe it feels. There’s no stress, no danger, just quiet progress and gentle storytelling. And yet, it still manages to make you feel things. The only downside? It’s short. Most people finish it in around 3–4 hours . But honestly, it feels less like a long-term game and more like a beautiful experience you revisit when you need comfort.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features passive storytelling through environmental details and the arrangement of objects across different life stages.

citations.review_text:
A cute and relaxing pixel organizing game. It's one of those games where you can just turn your brain off after a long day! Although I highly recommend picking this game up at a discount due to the amount of content this game offers. Other than that, this was an enjoyable experience for me. The aesthetics of this game is very pleasing and pretty to look at, while the soundtracks are effective at setting out a serene mood. I originally picked up this game because it looked cozy, but what made me love this game even more while playing was the passive storytelling through the environment! Most interactable objects in the game tell a story itself, whether it's not through the setting or the quick little P.S. after a level completion. And the ending is SOO WHOLESOME!!! A great game to organize and relax!

P.S. There is a setting where you can place items anywhere for those who want to know!

Absolute recommend. Cute visual style, fun organization and decorating, and it's fun to imagine the story as you play including trying to sort out what sentimental reasons lead to some items carrying over between the years, and it's fun to replay to see if you can find different ways to organize things than how you did it the last time.

Also, ngl, insanely cathartic to put up the college degree each time after the boyfriend apartment segment.

I'm at the part where I moved back in with my parents after a bad breakup and this game has been helping me heal by remembering it is ok to start over again and be on my own. Thank you to the creators for this game, even if its not "trendy" anymore.
